methods.label: Split the areas and match boundary lengths
methods.explanation:
[Figure 1](figures/2000_AMC_8_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

Use the distance between adjacent pegs in a row or column as one unit. Quadrilateral \(I\) is a parallelogram whose vertical base has length \(1\). Its opposite vertical side is \(1\) unit away horizontally, so its area is
\[
1\cdot1=1.
\]
For quadrilateral \(II\), name its vertices \(P,Q,R,S\) in boundary order, starting at the leftmost vertex: \(Q\) is the upper-right vertex, \(R\) is the inward corner, and \(S\) is the bottom vertex. Draw the horizontal segment \(PR\). It has length \(1\) and splits the quadrilateral into triangles \(PQR\) and \(PRS\). Their vertices \(Q\) and \(S\) lie one grid row above and below \(PR\), respectively. The triangles fill the quadrilateral without overlapping interiors, so its area is
\[
\frac{1\cdot1}{2}+\frac{1\cdot1}{2}=1.
\]
Thus the areas are equal.

For the perimeters, let \(d\) be the length of a diagonal of one grid square and let \(\ell=PQ\). Each figure has two sides of length \(d\). The other two sides of \(I\) each have length \(1\), while those of \(II\) have lengths \(1\) and \(\ell\). Hence
\[
P_I=2d+2,\qquad P_{II}=2d+1+\ell.
\]
The endpoints of \(PQ\) are two grid columns apart. Their horizontal separation is \(2\), and a segment cannot be shorter than that perpendicular separation, so \(\ell\ge2>1\). Therefore
\[
P_{II}-P_I=\ell-1>0.
\]
The figures have equal areas, and \(I\) has the smaller perimeter, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: The pixels confirm that I has vertical base 1 and horizontal height 1. In II, PR is a unit horizontal interior diagonal, and Q and S have perpendicular heights 1 on opposite sides, giving area 1/2+1/2=1. Both perimeters contain two unit-square diagonals and one unit side. Their remaining sides are 1 and PQ respectively; PQ spans two columns, so PQ≥2>1. Thus II has greater perimeter, choice E.
